title: JEPA
question: Do the similarities and differences between PMAX and JEPA support Schmidhuber's claim that JEPA repeats the earlier method?

usual_credit.summary: Yann LeCun proposed the Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) in his 2022 position paper 'A Path Towards Autonomous Machine Intelligence', in which two encoders map related inputs to representations and a predictor learns to predict one representation from the other instead of predicting raw pixels. Meta's I-JEPA (2023) implements the idea for images, and LeCun's company AMI Labs is built around world models.

claim.summary: Schmidhuber says JEPA is essentially identical to the Predictability Maximization (PMAX) family that he and his student Daniel Prelinger published in 1992-93. In PMAX, two non-generative networks interact so that one creates an informative latent representation of its input that the other network can predict from its own latent representation, with measures against what is now called collapse. He says the 1992 paper reported experiments, including a stereo task on which it outperformed Becker and Hinton's earlier IMAX, and that LeCun did not cite it. He adds that Michal Valko, who led the BYOL team, told him that later methods such as Barlow Twins and VICReg correspond to sections of the 1992 paper.

response.summary: LeCun argues that joint-embedding architectures were introduced decades ago and that JEPA's contribution must be assessed through its prediction objective, collapse prevention and practical results, not the broad two-encoder pattern alone. He points to Becker and Hinton's work as an earlier source and disputes Schmidhuber's invention claim. His X and April 2026 LinkedIn posts state that position directly; the separate 6 April comment and criticism of PMAX's experiments are reproduced on Schmidhuber's page rather than linked to their originals. Those reproduced remarks and Schmidhuber's rebuttal should therefore be read with that provenance in mind.

agreed_facts: Schmidhuber and Prelinger's 'Discovering predictable classifications' appeared in Neural Computation 5(4) in 1993, based on a 1992 technical report.
Becker and Hinton's work on maximizing mutual information between representations of related inputs, from a 1989 technical report, is an earlier joint-embedding method, and both sides cite it.
LeCun posted 'A Path Towards Autonomous Machine Intelligence' on OpenReview on 27 June 2022, and he describes it as a position paper.
The first image-based implementation, I-JEPA, was posted on arXiv on 19 January 2023.
Siamese networks were introduced at NIPS 1993 by Bromley, Guyon, LeCun, Säckinger and Shah.
crux: The dispute is over whether JEPA, as a class of architectures with a latent-space predictor and anti-collapse training, is the same as the 1992 PMAX family, as Schmidhuber argues, or an extension of earlier joint-embedding methods such as Becker and Hinton's, as LeCun argues. LeCun puts the weight on how collapse is prevented and on scaling. A further question is whether leaving PMAX out of the 2022 paper was a failure to credit, given that LeCun's own account names Becker and Hinton as the origin.

card.headline: JEPA
card.question: Is LeCun's 2022 JEPA essentially the same idea as the 1992 PMAX system?
card.claim: He says his 1992 PMAX trained two networks so that one predicts the other's internal representation, and that LeCun did not cite it.
card.pushback: LeCun says JEPA names a class of architectures going back to Becker and Hinton's 1989 work, and that Schmidhuber did not invent it either.
card.crux: The question is whether JEPA matches PMAX specifically, or only shares a general design going back to Becker and Hinton's 1989 work.
